Subject: GPU shelf-life & burst allocation playbook — clarifying autoscale exceptions

Team —

Quick context: NovaMed is locking in a 9-month dedicated pilot (NM-2027-06-PILOT-88). They want a short runway for burst capacity during weekly inference spikes (peak 3–5 hours/day). Procurement asked us to document how "temporary burst lanes" are governed and what qualifies for an autoscale exception versus standard reserved capacity.

Attached: burst_sla_matrix.xlsx (draft), proposed_runbook.md (outline), cost-sensitivity-snapshot.pdf (estimates).

Asks:
- Product: can we define the product-level guardrails for granting a temporary autoscale exception (metrics, approval path, and rollback criteria)?
- Infra/Runtime (Karthik): what are the kernel/sequence length limitations we should call out (i.e., when a burst lane would materially affect other tenants)?
- Ops (Marcus): what capacity buffers are realistic to promise for a 9-month pilot without breaking safety bands?
- Finance/Procurement (David): what wording do you need for the SOW to reflect temporary burst lanes vs committed slices?

Goal: have a short playbook and approval flow we can hand to NovaMed legal/procurement by EOD Friday. If we can’t meet that, propose a fallback — I’ll schedule a 30-min sync day after tomorrow.

Thanks —
Laura Bennett
Sr. Product Manager, Dedicated
Redwood Inference

Subject: Re: GPU shelf-life & burst allocation playbook — clarifying autoscale exceptions

Laura —

Thanks for the clear asks. High-level guardrail proposal from Product:

- Eligibility: Pilot customers on a committed minimum (>= 3 months) can request a temporary burst lane up to 20% additional throughput for windows not exceeding 8 hours/day and 3 days/week.
- Approval path: Product -> Infra (capacity check) -> Finance (cost approval) -> Head of Dedicated (final sign-off).
- Metrics required with request: historical QPS, peak 95th latency, token-distribution sketch, and a test canary run (5–10% traffic) for 24 hours.
- Rollback criteria: sustained 95th-latency > 1.5x baseline for 30 minutes OR error-rate > 0.5% sustained for 15 minutes.

Open questions for Karthik: what constitutes a "kernel-sensitive" workload where we should disallow burst (e.g., very long sequences or large KV-cache footprints)? Also, we should include a canary config in the runbook so infra can flip back automatically.

If this looks ok, I can draft the Product section of the runbook and push a version to the shared drive.

-Kimberly
VP, Product — Dedicated
Redwood Inference

Laura / all —

Technical constraints to bake into the playbook:

- Kernel/sequence sensitivities: workloads with median sequence length > 1024 or heavy per-token KV cache (>3GB per model shard) materially increase tail latency when co-located with mixed workloads. For those, we should either require dedicated slice isolation or limit bursts to cold-start-only (not steady-state).
- Autoscale semantics: prefer prefabricated "burst lanes" (pre-provisioned ephemeral slices) rather than broad cluster overcommit. Burst lanes should be pinned to specific rack/zone groups to avoid noisy neighbors.
- Canary approach: 1-hour canary at 10% traffic with full tracing enabled + prefix cache warm-up. If canary passes, we allow progressive ramp to requested burst level with automatic abort on rollback criteria.
- Monitoring hooks: make sure console exposes per-tenant 95th token latency and KV cache pressure so Product/Ops can see live impact.

I can work with Ops to propose the pinning matrix (which racks/zones) and an ops-runbook snippet. Recommend we disallow bursts that would require model re-quantization or specialized kernels during the pilot.

-Karthik
Senior Staff Engineer, Inference Runtime
Redwood Inference

All —

From an Ops/cost perspective:

- Short answer: we can promise a 15% burst buffer for up to 6 hours/day without touching long-term safety bands for a 9-month pilot, assuming the workloads are standard-gen autoregressive models. 20% is doable but requires either extra pre-provisioned slots or a higher price point in the SOW.
- Pre-provisioning vs on-demand: pre-provisioned ephemeral slices (pre-warmed) cost ~30% less from a tail-latency standpoint than live spin-up during a spike. For NovaMed, if they want guaranteed low 95th latency during bursts, we should recommend pre-provisioned ephemeral slices in the proposal.
- Ops checklist to include in runbook: rack pinning table, warm-up checklist, canary run playbook, fallback play (live traffic diversion to hosted model variant), and contact list for emergency eviction.

Related: I linked our draft playbook and JIRA ticket where we'll track the operational checklist: JIRA-DEDIC-3421.

Happy to run a 30-min ops drill with NovaMed next week to walk through failure cases.

-Marcus
Head of Dedicated Operations

Laura —

For SOW language, procurement wants two clear sections: (1) committed capacity (slices + uptime SLA) and (2) temporary burst lanes (description + pricing table + approval cadence). Suggested phrasing in the SOW: "Temporary Burst Lanes: Customer may request short-duration burst capacity as a temporary augmentation to committed slices. Each request must include a ramp plan and canary; Redwood will evaluate against kernel sensitivity and capacity and provide approval or counter-offer within 48 hours. Pricing is based on pre-provisioned slice equivalence at X% premium or on-demand at Y% premium."

I can draft the procurement paragraph and the pricing table if Product/Ops confirm the guardrails (Kimberly + Marcus + Karthik). I also need the final list of JIRA items and the drive link to the runbook.

-David
